Which assumptions connect market observations to a merger prediction? This
reference explains demand, conduct, and the posterior state retained in policy
calculations. Start with the executable [PNB example](pnb-merger.html) ([source](https://github.com/luciu5/antitrustBayes/blob/main/vignettes/pnb-merger.Rmd)); the
optional [posterior workflow](posterior-workflow.html) ([source](https://github.com/luciu5/antitrustBayes/blob/main/vignettes/posterior-workflow.Rmd)) shows estimation and
paired scenarios. The only computation here is a small deterministic
conduct-information example; no inference or statistical validation runs.

## Units and market-side conventions

Logit observes quantity shares. CES estimation also observes quantities and
converts them to revenue shares for supply equations. Write $s_j$ for an
unconditional quantity share, $r_j$ for an unconditional revenue share, and
$s_0,r_0$ for their outside shares. Conditional inside shares satisfy
$s_j=(1-s_0)s_{j|I}$ and $r_j=(1-r_0)r_{j|I}$. A firm's share sums the shares
of **all its products**; product share alone is insufficient for multiproduct
conduct.

Output-market Lerner margins are $m_j=(p_j-c_j)/p_j$, with marginal cost $c_j$.
In an input deposit market the positive markdown instead is
$m_j=(v_j-p_j)/p_j$, where $v_j$ is the value-of-funds primitive and $p_j$ is
the deposit rate. Markdown ratios can exceed one. A lower output price benefits
buyers; a lower deposit rate harms depositors. Level-rate changes and relative
rate changes have different units.

The Bayesian Logit parameter $\alpha$ is a **positive magnitude**. The output
utility slope is $-\alpha$; the input utility slope is $+\alpha$. This differs
from the signed output-Logit slope in `antitrust`. Current CES estimation
supports output markets only; Logit supports input and output markets.

## Demand and outside normalization

For output Logit, normalized choice probabilities have the form

$$
s_j=\frac{\exp(b_j-\alpha p_j+\mu)}
 {1+\sum_l\exp(b_l-\alpha p_l+\mu)}.
$$

The outside utility is zero. For input Logit, replace $-\alpha p_j$ with
$+\alpha p_j$. Product quality and the market-level normalization determine
attractiveness as well as price sensitivity.

A CES revenue-share representation uses positive quality weights $a_j$ and
$\gamma>1$, with $r_j$ proportional to $a_jp_j^{1-\gamma}$, including an
outside good at price $p_0$. Quantity shares follow by dividing revenue shares
by prices and renormalizing. The weights are not numerically interchangeable
with Logit quality coefficients. If $\bar p_I$ is the inside
quantity-weighted price, outside quantity and revenue shares are related by

$$
r_0=\frac{s_0p_0}{s_0p_0+(1-s_0)\bar p_I}.
$$

Consequently, a market-shared outside quantity share can imply different outside
revenue shares over time when prices change. The outside price must use the
same units as inside prices. The estimated outside share is latent, not a
supplied empirical market-penetration observation.

## What the posterior and a policy plan retain

The current Gaussian relative-share likelihood uses orthonormal contrasts of
log conditional inside **quantity** shares. It removes their common level;
it does not observe aggregate inside-market attractiveness. Persistent product
quality is centered within its market and shared across periods. Under the
default collapsed parameterization, it is integrated during inference and
recovered conditionally when constructing a policy plan.

Specification 15's default `share_residual_model = "demand_shock"` additionally
separates period demand shocks from independent measurement error. Joint
share/margin dependence belongs to the prescribed likelihood; independent
measurement noise is a separate observation component. The measurement SD has
a configurable Lognormal prior with median .10 and log SD .5. A snapshot need
not identify the demand/measurement variance split well; apparent precision
can depend on those priors.

`posterior_policy_draws()` jointly retains the parameter draw, persistent
quality, recovered period demand, outside-share normalization and any latent
role realization. The derived market-year intercept reproduces that draw's
outside share at reference prices; relative-share fits have no free intercept
prior. Policy demand keeps quality **plus period demand**, while measurement
noise stays in the observation model. These are states for the fitted period,
not fresh shocks drawn independently for each scenario.

Estimated-fit simulation defaults to `demand_anchoring = "latent_quality"`.
It reconstructs a pre-policy equilibrium, which generally differs from observed
prices/shares, then measures the policy change from that same draw's baseline.
Reusing one plan aligns states across scenarios. Explicit `"observed"` retains
the older conditional observed-share calibration and does not change inference
or model weights. Supplied-state fits have their own calibration route and no
estimated quality posterior.

Compatible specification-14 fits keep their original residual interpretation.
New fits can explicitly select `"combined"`; absolute-share likelihoods retain
their original residual model. New-model weights require new inference and
evidence. See `?bayes_est`, `?posterior_policy_draws` and `?bayes_sim` for the
supported configurations and state contracts.

## Conduct and portfolio first-order conditions

Let $S_f=\sum_{l\in\mathcal J_f}s_l$ and
$R_f=\sum_{l\in\mathcal J_f}r_l$ denote unconditional firm shares. The table
expresses the standard output-market proportional margins. The input Logit
route uses the positive markdown and input-price sign convention above.

| Conduct | Logit margin $m_j$ | CES margin $m_j$ |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Monopolistic competition | $1/(\alpha p_j)$ | $1/\gamma$ |
| Bertrand | $1/\{\alpha p_j(1-S_f)\}$ | $1/\{\gamma-(\gamma-1)R_f\}$ |
| Cournot | $(s_0+S_f)/(\alpha p_js_0)$ | $1/\gamma+(\gamma-1)R_f/[\gamma\{1+(\gamma-1)r_0\}]$ |
| Second-score auction | $-\log(1-S_f)/(\alpha p_jS_f)$ | $1-(1-R_f)^{1/(\gamma-1)}$ |

Bertrand firms choose portfolio prices and internalize recaptured sales.
Cournot firms choose quantities and account for inverse demand. Monopolistic
competition uses perceived own demand, holding the aggregate denominator/index
fixed. Auction conduct describes competition for contracts with a second-score
payment rule. An institution must support that interpretation; it is not an
automatically plausible model of every retail deposit market. The default
banking candidate prior therefore downweights it.

Nash bargaining is an additional API option, outside the baseline banking
candidate set. Let $\beta$ be buyer-side bargaining power and
$\kappa=\beta/(1-\beta)$. Its schedules are

$$
m_j^{\mathrm{Logit}}=
 \frac{-\log(1-S_f)}{\alpha p_j\{\kappa S_f-(1-S_f)\log(1-S_f)\}},
\qquad
m_j^{\mathrm{CES}}=\frac{1-\beta}{\gamma-(\gamma-1)R_f}.
$$

The Bayesian multiproduct Logit bargaining schedule intentionally differs from
`antitrust`'s registered product-level bargaining system, so that case retains
its explicit Bayesian conduct class. CES bargaining scales its Bertrand
schedule; free demand scale and bargaining power can be confounded. The baseline
power prior is neutral on $[0,.9999)$; a high-power prior is a sensitivity choice.
Model-specific recovery and cost/value-of-funds conventions remain fixed when
comparing policy anchoring.

## Local conversions are not global equivalence

Logging multiplicative utility with Fréchet taste shocks gives Gumbel errors
and a **log-price** utility index. It preserves the CES choice probabilities;
replacing log price by price changes the demand model. For an output market,
matching the CES log-price derivative to linear-price Logit at one reference
price gives

$$
\alpha=(\gamma-1)/p_{\mathrm{ref}}.
$$

This is a local reference-price comparison. At unequal product prices the local
derivatives differ by product, so the formula cannot make a single common-alpha
Logit globally equivalent to CES. `?wtp_convert` uses a reference-price
conversion; it is not a theorem about identical substitution or merger effects.

## What share geometry can reveal about conduct

One inverse-margin observation can often be matched by changing a demand scale.
Different firm shares reveal the shape of a conduct schedule, but uncertainty
about the outside share can make distinct schedules harder to separate. Reuse
a small deterministic schedule geometry to compare known and profiled outside
shares:

```{r conduct-information}
library(antitrustBayes)
q <- c(.03, .08, .15, .25)
known <- conduct_distance(q, "cournot", "bertrand", s0_k = .2,
                          profile_s0 = FALSE)
unknown <- conduct_distance(q, "cournot", "bertrand", s0_k = .2,
                            profile_s0 = TRUE)
c(known_outside = known$distance, profiled_outside = unknown$distance)
```

Here the two distances agree to the displayed precision. Profiling enlarges
the comparison model's choices, so the minimized distance cannot increase; it
need not fall strictly for every share geometry. This Gaussian/KL approximation describes local information,
not posterior model recovery or statistical coverage. Firm shares must be
jointly feasible: `sum(q) <= 1-s0` (tolerance `1e-8`); `q` may enumerate only a
subset of firms. A profiled outside share is bounded by `1-sum(q)`.

Use `?conduct_information_matrix` for pairwise comparisons and
`?conduct_validation` for a separately requested, potentially expensive Monte
Carlo study. Neither is required for the merger workflows.
